question: What is the statutory definition of a "brokerage agreement" under Iowa Code section 543B.5(7)?
choice_a: An oral or written understanding between a buyer and seller regarding closing costs
choice_b: A contract between a broker and a client establishing the parties' relationship and the broker's compensation for services, containing the provisions required by section 543B.56A
choice_c: A standard form promulgated exclusively by the Iowa Real Estate Commission that all brokers must use
choice_d: A disclosure statement identifying which party a broker represents in a transaction
explanation: Iowa Code 543B.5(7) defines "brokerage agreement" as a contract between a broker and a client which establishes the relationship between the parties as to, and the broker's compensation for, the brokerage services to be performed, and requires it to contain the provisions mandated by section 543B.56A. Choice D actually describes an "agency disclosure" under 543B.5(2), a related but separate concept, and Iowa does not require use of a single commission-issued statewide brokerage agreement form.

question: Under Iowa Code section 543B.56A(2), a written brokerage agreement must specify that the broker will, at minimum, do all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: Accept delivery of and present to the client offers and counteroffers
choice_b: Assist the client in developing, communicating, negotiating, and presenting offers until the transaction is completed or contingencies are resolved
choice_c: Guarantee the sale of the property within a fixed time period or forfeit the broker's commission
choice_d: Conspicuously disclose that the broker's compensation, fees, and commission are negotiable and not established by law
explanation: Section 543B.56A(2) lists specific minimum broker obligations: accepting and presenting offers/counteroffers, assisting the client through negotiation to completion, answering the client's questions, providing buyer access to listed properties, and conspicuously disclosing that compensation is negotiable and not fixed by law. Nothing in Iowa law requires -- or permits as standard practice -- a broker to guarantee a sale within a fixed period or forfeit the commission; that is not among the enumerated statutory duties.

question: Under Iowa Code section 543B.56A(3), when must a written brokerage agreement generally be signed by both broker and client in a seller representation, absent an applicable exception?
choice_a: At closing, before disbursement of proceeds
choice_b: Within 10 days after the property is placed on the MLS
choice_c: At any point before the final walk-through
choice_d: Prior to the broker listing any property for sale on behalf of the seller
explanation: Section 543B.56A(3) requires the brokerage agreement to be signed by both broker and client before the broker lists any property for sale on behalf of a seller, before showing a property to a buyer, or (if no property is shown) before making an offer on a property on behalf of a buyer.

question: Which of the following buyer scenarios is specifically EXEMPTED from Iowa's requirement that a buyer's representation agreement be signed before a licensee shows property, under Iowa Code section 543B.56A(3)?
choice_a: A customer attending an open house or an auction
choice_b: A buyer who has already made three unsuccessful offers on other properties
choice_c: A buyer purchasing a single-family home under $150,000
choice_d: A buyer who is also a licensed real estate salesperson
explanation: Section 543B.56A(3) exempts customers attending an open house or auction, potential buyers of a property with more than four dwelling units, and properties not intended for human habitation from the buyer-side brokerage agreement signing requirement. Purchase price and the buyer's own licensure status are irrelevant to the exemption.

question: Under Iowa Code section 543B.45, a licensee who knowingly makes, issues, or permits the use of two or more contracts for the sale of the same parcel -- one of which is concealed from the prospective lender to enable the purchaser to obtain a larger loan -- has committed what?
choice_a: A simple misdemeanor only, with no other consequence
choice_b: A fraudulent practice
choice_c: An act that is permissible if disclosed to the buyer only
choice_d: A civil infraction subject solely to a $100 fine
explanation: Iowa Code 543B.45 prohibits "dual contracts" for the sale of the same parcel where one contract is concealed from the prospective lender or loan guarantor to enable the purchaser to obtain a larger loan than the true sales price would allow, or to qualify for a loan the purchaser could not otherwise obtain, and expressly declares a violation to be a "fraudulent practice" (cross-referencing Iowa Code 714.8) -- a more serious classification than a simple misdemeanor or minor civil infraction.

question: Iowa Administrative Code rule 193E-11.1(4) prohibits a licensee from entering into a "net listing agreement." What is a net listing, and what is the consequence of taking one in Iowa?
choice_a: A listing with no expiration date; the listing is automatically voided after 90 days
choice_b: A listing where the seller pays no commission at all; it is expressly permitted with written seller consent
choice_c: An agreement specifying a net sale price to the owner with any excess going to the broker as commission; taking one is unprofessional conduct violating Iowa Code sections 543B.29(3) and 543B.34(8)
choice_d: An agreement where the buyer's agent nets a flat referral fee; it requires commission pre-approval from the commission
explanation: IAC 193E-11.1(4) defines a net listing as an agreement specifying a net price to be received by the owner, with the broker keeping any amount above that price as commission, and expressly states that taking such a listing is unprofessional conduct constituting a violation of Iowa Code sections 543B.29(3) (unethical/harmful conduct) and 543B.34(8) (grounds for civil penalty and license sanction).

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.1, every Iowa listing agreement must contain certain minimum elements. Which of the following is explicitly PROHIBITED from being included in the listing?
choice_a: The commission to be paid
choice_b: A definite expiration date
choice_c: The signatures of all parties concerned
choice_d: A provision requiring the seller to notify the broker of the seller's intent to cancel the listing after the stated expiration date
explanation: IAC 193E-11.1 requires listing agreements to include the price, commission, signatures of all parties, and a definite expiration date, but expressly states the agreement "shall contain no provision requiring a party signing the listing to notify the broker of the listing party's intention to cancel the listing after such definite expiration date" -- protecting sellers from an automatic post-expiration renewal trap.

question: To enforce a "protective clause" (a holdover/tail provision) beyond the expiration of an exclusive listing under Iowa rules, what must the broker do?
choice_a: Provide the listing party, in writing and prior to expiration, the names and available contact information of persons to whom the property was presented during the listing term, delivered by personal service with acknowledgment or by both regular and certified mail
choice_b: Nothing further; protective clauses are self-executing upon listing expiration
choice_c: File the protective clause with the Iowa Real Estate Commission for approval
choice_d: Obtain a notarized affidavit from the buyer's agent confirming no other offers exist
explanation: IAC 193E-11.2 requires that a protective (safety) clause be provided for in the listing contract with a definite protection period, and requires the broker, in writing and prior to expiration, to furnish the listing party the names and available contact information of persons to whom the property was presented during the active listing term for whom protection is sought, delivered either by personal service with written acknowledgment of receipt or by both regular mail and certified mail, return receipt requested.

question: IAC rule 193E-11.3(2)-(3) extends the net-agreement prohibition beyond simple listings. What does this rule prohibit?
choice_a: Any brokerage agreement that does not name a specific closing agent
choice_b: Any brokerage agreement (not just a listing) specifying a net sale, lease, rental, or exchange price to the owner with the excess to the licensee as commission
choice_c: Any brokerage agreement lasting longer than 180 days
choice_d: Any brokerage agreement involving more than one buyer
explanation: IAC 193E-11.3(2) broadens the net listing prohibition to cover all brokerage agreements -- seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant representation, not merely seller listings -- and 193E-11.3(3) confirms that taking a net brokerage agreement is unprofessional conduct harmful to the public, violating Iowa Code sections 543B.29(3) and 543B.34(8).

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.3(6)(a), does the identity of the party who actually pays a broker's compensation in an Iowa transaction (buyer, seller, landlord, tenant, or third party) determine who the broker legally represents?
choice_a: Yes; whoever pays is automatically deemed the broker's client
choice_b: Only if the payment exceeds 3% of the sale price
choice_c: No; payment of compensation does not establish or determine an agency relationship
choice_d: Only in commercial transactions, not residential transactions
explanation: IAC 193E-11.3(6)(a) explicitly provides that payment of compensation "shall not be construed to determine or establish an agency relationship" -- a broker's compensation in a transaction may be paid by the seller, buyer, landlord, tenant, a third party, or by splitting/sharing compensation between cooperating brokers, without the source of that payment dictating whom the broker represents.

question: Where should a commission-split agreement between a listing broker and a cooperating (selling) broker be documented under Iowa rules, and can a buyer's offer be conditioned on it?
choice_a: It may be written directly into the purchase agreement as a standard clause
choice_b: It must be recorded with the county recorder along with the deed
choice_c: It is unenforceable in Iowa under any circumstances
choice_d: It should be a separate document, and a purchase agreement should not be made contingent on the selling broker receiving a specific percentage of the listing broker's commission
explanation: IAC 193E-11.3(10) provides that a commission-split agreement between brokers "should be a separate document and not included in the purchase agreement," and that a purchase agreement should not be made contingent on the selling broker receiving a certain percentage of the listing broker's commission -- keeping inter-broker compensation disputes separate from the buyer-seller contract.

question: Under Iowa's brokerage agreement and listing rules, once the parties to a listing or brokerage agreement have agreed on a commission or fee, may a licensee who is not a party to that agreement attempt to alter, modify, or change it?
choice_a: No -- not without the prior written consent of the parties to that listing or brokerage agreement
choice_b: Yes, at any time, as a matter of professional courtesy
choice_c: Only with the Iowa Real Estate Commission's prior approval
choice_d: Yes, but only within 10 days of the agreement's signing
explanation: IAC 193E-11.1(6) and 11.3(8)-(9) prohibit any licensee who is not a party to a listing or brokerage agreement from attempting to alter, modify, or change -- or inducing another to alter, modify, or change -- a previously agreed-upon commission or fee, without the prior written consent of the parties to that agreement.

question: Under Iowa Code section 543B.34(1)(i), a broker generally may not pay a commission or other consideration to a person who is not a licensed Iowa broker or salesperson for performing licensed acts. Which of the following IS a recognized statutory exception?
choice_a: Payment to any friend or family member of the broker who assisted informally
choice_b: Payment to the estate or heirs of a deceased licensee who held a valid license when the commission was earned
choice_c: Payment to any unlicensed marketing consultant who generated the lead
choice_d: Payment to a home inspector who referred the client
explanation: Iowa Code 543B.34(1)(i)(1) generally prohibits paying commissions or consideration to unlicensed persons for acts requiring licensure, but carves out narrow exceptions, including payment of earned commissions to the estate or heirs of a deceased licensee who held a valid Iowa real estate license at the time the commission was earned, certain foreign referral agents, and certain wholly-owned corporations of a licensee meeting specified statutory conditions.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.4, who bears responsibility for ensuring that preprinted contract forms and documents used by an Iowa brokerage comply with Iowa real estate law and commission rules?
choice_a: The Iowa Real Estate Commission, which pre-approves every form used statewide
choice_b: The buyer's attorney exclusively
choice_c: The broker
choice_d: The title company handling the closing
explanation: IAC 193E-11.4 states a licensee shall not write, prepare, or use a contract containing terms or conditions that violate Iowa Code chapter 543B or commission rules, and specifically places responsibility on the broker to ensure that all preprinted documents and forms used by the brokerage comply with these rules. Iowa does not operate a single commission-mandated statewide contract form that resolves this obligation for brokers.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.5, after execution of a real estate contract instrument, what must a licensee do, and how long must the broker retain copies?
choice_a: Deliver copies only if a party specifically requests one in writing; retain for one year
choice_b: Mail copies only to the buyer; retain indefinitely
choice_c: No delivery obligation exists once the deal closes; retain for 30 days
choice_d: Deliver a legible copy to each party as soon as practicable; the broker must retain copies for five years
explanation: IAC 193E-11.5 requires a licensee, upon execution of any instrument in connection with a real estate transaction, to deliver a legible copy of the original instrument to each party as soon as practicable, placing responsibility on the licensee to prepare sufficient copies, and requires the broker to retain copies for five years.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.6(1), may a licensee pay a referral fee or finder's fee to an unlicensed third party for performing functions that require an Iowa real estate license?
choice_a: No -- referral fees or finder's fees paid to unlicensed third parties for performing brokerage activities are prohibited
choice_b: Yes, as long as it is disclosed to both parties in the contract
choice_c: Yes, up to a maximum of $500 per transaction
choice_d: Yes, but only for commercial (not residential) transactions
explanation: IAC 193E-11.6(1) prohibits a licensee from paying a commission, any part of a commission, or other valuable consideration to an unlicensed third party for performing brokerage functions or engaging in any activity that requires an Iowa real estate license; referral fees or finder's fees paid to unlicensed third parties for such activities are expressly prohibited, with no dollar-amount safe harbor.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-11.7, when a builder's contract will attach personal property or a structure to land (producing an improvement to real estate), what must a licensee disclose, and does the type of representation the licensee provides matter?
choice_a: Nothing needs to be disclosed if the licensee represents neither party to the transaction
choice_b: The licensee must disclose in writing that the licensee and the broker/brokerage will receive commission or compensation for the transaction, and this disclosure is required regardless of the type of representation provided -- or even if no representation is provided
choice_c: Disclosure is required only if the licensee's commission exceeds 6% of the contract price
choice_d: Disclosure is only required when representing the seller, not the buyer
explanation: IAC 193E-11.7 treats a builder's contract to construct or attach a structure to land as a real estate transaction, and requires the licensee to make a written disclosure revealing that the licensee and the licensee's brokerage will receive a commission, compensation, or other valuable consideration for the transaction. This written-disclosure duty applies "regardless of the type of representation provided by the licensee or if the licensee provides no representation."

question: Iowa Code section 543B.6A, addressing "wholesaling" of residential property, requires a wholesaler to disclose certain information in writing to all parties before executing a contract to purchase or convey the equitable interest. If the wholesaler fails to make this disclosure, what remedy does the statute give the seller or buyer?
choice_a: The contract remains fully binding regardless of the disclosure failure
choice_b: Only the Iowa Real Estate Commission may void the contract, not the parties themselves
choice_c: The seller or buyer may cancel the contract at any time prior to closing without penalty, and may retain any earnest money paid by the wholesaler
choice_d: The wholesaler is entitled to specific performance regardless of the disclosure failure
explanation: Iowa Code 543B.6A(3)(a) requires a wholesaler to disclose the legal identities of all parties and an explanation of the wholesaling process (including that the wholesaler holds only an equitable, not legal, interest and may be unable to convey title) before executing a contract to purchase or convey. Under 543B.6A(3)(c), if the wholesaler fails to comply with this disclosure requirement, the seller or buyer may cancel the contract at any time prior to closing without penalty, and may retain any earnest money the wholesaler paid.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-7.15, what is a listing broker's obligation regarding back-up offers once the seller has accepted a written offer to purchase, absent a contrary written agreement?
choice_a: The listing broker may refuse to present any further offers once one has been accepted
choice_b: Back-up offers are automatically void once the primary offer is accepted
choice_c: The listing broker must forward back-up offers only if the primary buyer's financing is denied
choice_d: The listing broker must continue to present back-up offers to the seller until the transaction has closed, unless the seller and broker have agreed in writing otherwise
explanation: IAC 193E-7.15 requires that all written offers to purchase be promptly presented to the seller for formal acceptance or rejection, and, unless there is a written agreement between the seller and the listing broker directing otherwise, requires the listing broker to continue presenting back-up offers until the transaction has closed.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-7.15(1), before a customer's agent (an agent seeking compensation from the listing broker) prepares an offer to purchase on a listed property, what must occur?
choice_a: The customer's agent must first obtain authorization and agreement from the listing broker
choice_b: Nothing; any agent may prepare and submit an offer freely on any listed property
choice_c: The customer's agent must file a notice of intent with the Iowa Real Estate Commission
choice_d: The customer's agent must secure a surety bond equal to the earnest money amount
explanation: IAC 193E-7.15(1) requires a customer's agent seeking compensation from the listing broker to first obtain authorization and agreement from the listing broker before preparing an offer to purchase on the property the listing broker represents.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-7.15(3), immediately upon receiving a signed and dated offer to purchase from a buyer (with any accompanying consideration), what must the listing agent do?
choice_a: Hold the offer confidentially until the seller responds, with no obligation to inform the buyer
choice_b: Provide a copy of the offer to purchase to the buyer as a receipt
choice_c: Forward the offer only to the buyer's lender for verification
choice_d: Wait 24 hours before acknowledging receipt of the offer
explanation: IAC 193E-7.15(3) requires the listing agent, immediately upon receiving an offer to purchase signed and dated by the buyer (with consideration, if any), to provide a copy of the offer to purchase to the buyer as a receipt.

question: Under IAC rule 193E-13.4, when an offer to purchase is withdrawn or an acceptance is revoked without liability under Iowa Code chapter 558A (the property disclosure law), is the seller's consent required before the broker returns the earnest money deposit to the buyer?
choice_a: Yes, the seller must sign a written release before any funds are returned
choice_b: No, but only if the broker first obtains a court order
choice_c: No -- the earnest money deposit shall be promptly returned to the buyer without delay, and the seller's consent and agreement to release the funds is not required
choice_d: Yes, unless the seller has already vacated the property
explanation: IAC 193E-13.4 provides that when an offer is withdrawn or an acceptance revoked without liability under Iowa Code chapter 558A, any earnest money deposit must be promptly returned to the buyer without delay, and expressly states that the seller's consent and agreement to release the funds is not required -- a narrow, specific exception to Iowa's general rule that disputed earnest money otherwise requires mutual written agreement, a court judgment, or an interpleader action before disbursement.
source_note: Iowa Administrative Code 193E-13.4; Iowa Code chapter 558A

question: Iowa Court Rule 37.5, referenced in IAC rule 193E-13.2(8), authorizes nonlawyers (including real estate licensees, acting upon a buyer's or seller's written request) to select, prepare, and complete certain limited legal documents for a residential real estate transaction of four units or less. Which of the following documents are nonlawyers explicitly PROHIBITED from preparing under this rule?
choice_a: Groundwater hazard statements
choice_b: Offers to purchase or purchase agreements
choice_c: Declaration of value forms
choice_d: Deeds and real estate installment sales contracts
explanation: IAC 193E-13.2(8) explains that Iowa Ct. R. 37.5 permits nonlawyers, upon a buyer's or seller's written request, to select, prepare, and complete offers to purchase/purchase agreements (with a required written notice that these are binding legal documents and that competent legal advice should be sought), groundwater hazard statements, and declaration of value forms -- but nonlawyers may NOT select, prepare, or complete deeds, real estate installment sales contracts, affidavits of identity or nonidentity, affidavits of payment of spousal or child support, or other documents necessary to correct title problems or deficiencies; doing so beyond the rule's narrow scope constitutes the unauthorized practice of law.
source_note: Iowa Administrative Code 193E-13.2(8); Iowa Ct. R. 37.5

question: Under Iowa Code section 543B.3(9), which of the following categories of documents may generally only be prepared by a person acting within the statutory definition of a licensed "real estate broker" performing a brokerage act (subject to the narrow Iowa Ct. R. 37.5 nonlawyer carve-out)?
choice_a: Offers to purchase, purchase agreements, listing contracts, buyer's representation agreements, agency disclosures, and groundwater hazard statements (including modifications, amendments, or addendums)
choice_b: A simple grocery list attached to a home inspection report
choice_c: A homeowner's personal moving checklist
choice_d: A property's homeowners' association newsletter
explanation: Iowa Code 543B.3(9) defines the preparation of offers to purchase or purchase agreements, listing contracts, buyer's representation agreements, agency disclosures, real property residential and agricultural rental agreements, commercial rental agreements of one year or less, and groundwater hazard statements (including any modifications, amendments, or addendums to those specific documents) as an act constituting "dealing in real estate" requiring a broker's license, subject only to the narrow nonlawyer exception recognized under Iowa Ct. R. 37.5.

question: Does Iowa law provide residential real estate buyers a general statutory right of rescission or a mandatory "attorney review" period after signing a purchase agreement, comparable to provisions found in some other states?
choice_a: Yes, a 3-business-day right of rescission applies to every residential purchase agreement statewide
choice_b: No -- Iowa Code chapter 543B and the Iowa Administrative Code provide only narrow, specific cancellation rights (such as for a seller's failure to timely deliver the property disclosure statement required by chapter 558A, or a wholesaler's failure to make the disclosures required by section 543B.6A), not a general right of rescission or mandatory attorney-review period
choice_c: Yes, but only for purchase agreements exceeding $250,000
choice_d: No, because Iowa abolished earnest money contracts entirely in 2017
explanation: Unlike an attorney-review or cooling-off provision adopted in some other states, nothing in Iowa Code chapter 543B, chapter 558A, or the Iowa Administrative Code (193E) grants a blanket right of rescission for a signed residential purchase agreement. The only revocation/cancellation rights identified are narrow and situational: a buyer may revoke or withdraw an offer without liability if the seller's mandatory property disclosure statement under chapter 558A was not timely delivered (IAC 193E-14.1(3), 193E-13.4), and a seller or buyer may cancel a wholesale transaction contract before closing if the wholesaler failed to make the disclosures required by Iowa Code 543B.6A(3). There is no general rescission period, and Iowa has not abolished earnest money contracts.
source_note: Iowa Code chapter 558A; section 543B.6A(3); Iowa Administrative Code 193E-13.4, 193E-14.1(3) (no general rescission right identified in Iowa Code chapter 543B or IAC 193E)
